To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) HIV‐1 infection is a complex process that is regulated by multiple genetic and immunological factors and (ii) a better understanding of genetic determinants of susceptibility to HIV infection and AIDS will be of immense value in designing therapeutic vaccines and in developing novel antiviral strategies.
the CCR5Hhe carrying *59402 A allele is associated with increased risk of HIV‐1 transmission and development of AIDS.
genetic polymorphisms of HIV‐1 entry and immune genes have an impact on the outcome of infection in the Indian population.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms of host–virus interactions that could influence susceptibility and progression of HIV infection in Indian populations.
the role of genetic determinants of susceptibility to HIV infection and progression to disease, with special emphasis on chemokine receptors and their ligands.

the identification of genetic variants that could be used as biomarkers to identify people at higher risk of infection and disease progression, predict the rate of disease progression and response to antiretroviral therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are no ‘AIDS‐resistance genes’ per se, rather there are a multitude of genes that are associated with the risk of disease progression.
there are no single gene or genetic variants that are responsible for resistance or susceptibility to infection.
there is no ‘AIDS‐restriction gene,’ but rather a multitude of ‘AIDS‐restricting genes,’ each of which contributes to the complex genetic architecture of the disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Indian population is genetically distinct and has a different set of genes influencing susceptibility to HIV‐infection and progression to AIDS.
there is no single gene that determines susceptibility to HIV‐infection, but rather a combination of genetic variants and their interactions that influence the outcome of HIV infection.
genetic variability in HIV susceptibility and AIDS progression is complex, and the role of genetic factors in HIV‐1 infection is still not fully elucidated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Indian population, which has been considered to be relatively less susceptible to HIV infection, is in fact highly susceptible.
the Indian population is genetically distinct from the Caucasian population and that the genetic polymorphisms identified in the Indian population are different from the Caucasian population.
the genetic variants that could confer protection against HIV infection and limit disease progression vary among populations.
